Your poor dog — that 1 August and Silvester dread is real, and it's not just pets. Deer, horses, birds, and people with war trauma or PTSD all suffer from unpredictable explosions too.

If I'm honest: I'd vote yes. My reasoning — the harm from bang fireworks falls almost entirely on beings who never chose them (animals, neighbours, sleeping children), while the enjoyment goes to a relatively small group of private users on a few nights a year. And the "let each commune decide" approach doesn't work well in a country this size: drive twenty minutes across a cantonal border and you can buy what your town banned, and sound doesn't respect municipal boundaries anyway. A national rule ends the patchwork and the fireworks tourism. As I understand it, organised professional shows would still be possible, so the sky on the Bundesfeier wouldn't go dark.

The honest counterarguments: writing a ban into the constitution is a blunt, inflexible instrument — a normal law with a precise decibel threshold could be adjusted over time. Canton and communal rules have been tightening, buyers already have to register, and some people reasonably resist centralising yet another decision in Bern.

So: yes from me, though I wouldn't call a "no" vote unreasonable — it depends on whether you weigh the animal-protection case more heavily, or flexibility and local autonomy.

(One footnote: if we're talking about the actual Swiss vote of 29 November 2020, the initiative was rejected, with roughly 63.5% voting no.)

I can answer: for something whose harm occurs regardless of where you light it (sound carries, animals don't respect borders) and where local rules create purchasing arbitrage, a national rule makes sense — unlike, say, opening hours.
